newsitem.title: FRANCE: French PM Juppe made to show i.d. at polling booth.
newsitem.headline: French PM Juppe made to show i.d. at polling booth.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe ran into a hitch when he turned up to vote on Sunday in France's parliamentary election and a polling official demanded proof of his identity.

"Normally it's enough to be well known," the conservative Juppe objected in front of a barrage of photographers when the official asked for his identity card at a polling station in the southwestern city of Bordeaux.

"No, no, no, no! Everyone must show an identity card," the official replied. Juppe, who is mayor of the city as well as candidate in the National Assembly vote, got out his wallet and fumbled through banknotes to find his card.

Across France, voters went with apparently little enthusiasm to vote in the first round of the two-stage snap election. It followed a lacklustre campaign with President Jacques Chirac seeking a renewed mandate for his centre-right allies.
Newspapers have widely highlighted fears that many voters would take advantage of fine weather to leave home and spend a day in the sun.
In Paris, citizens crammed markets rather than polling stations.
At the food stalls lining the Rue Mouffetard, on the Left Bank, people queued up to buy champagne, smoked salmon and other delicacies for Mother's Day dinners.

At a polling station a few blocks away, voters straggled in one by one as voting got under way. A second, runoff round will take place next Sunday in districts where no one wins outright in the first.
"Parisians generally sleep in on Sundays, and then they go to the market, even on election day," said a woman checking in voters at a primary school on the Rue Buffon.
With official campaigning banned from Friday midnight, no one was allowed to pass out pamphlets on street corners, shake hands with voters or kiss babies.

News bulletins devoted most time to the conviction in northwestern France of a man who killed a nine-year-old girl by lacing her medicine with cyanide, mistaking her antibiotics for those of his mistress's husband.

Across Paris many of the candidates' posters, pasted up on official metal panels outside polling stations, were badly defaced or simply ripped. Insulting election graffiti, on the other hand, could be seen on nearly every wall.
"The Socialists ruined France," says one message spray-painted across the capital.

"Dump Tiberi," says another seemingly ubiquitous message, a reference to embattled Gaullist Paris mayor Jean Tiberi, who is seeking to retain his seat in the National Assembly although he and his wife are being probed on suspicion of political sleaze.

France's governing centre-right coalition held a huge majority in the outgoing assembly, and voter polls ahead of last weekend's publication blackout suggest it will retain a majority in the new parliament, albeit sharply reduced.
"To look at the crowds of people shopping, you would never know it was election day," mused an elderly woman handing out leaflets for an anti-racism organisation at a market in southwest Paris.
